channel.title: The Wine Reference: wine stories
channel.description: A new wine story every day by Diego Muntoni: history, people, places and curious facts.

item.title: The Twelve Grapes of Luck: Spain's New Year's Eve Ritual
item.description: Why Spaniards swallow a grape on every stroke of midnight, how a bit of Madrid mockery became a national rite, and the bagged Aledo grapes that make it possible.

item.title: The History of Mulled Wine: From Roman Conditum to Glühwein
item.description: Long before Christmas markets, Romans sweetened wine with honey and pepper, medieval cooks brewed hippocras and Dickens served Smoking Bishop. Here is how mulled wine became winter's drink.

item.title: Port and Stilton: Why Britain Pairs Them at Christmas
item.description: A sweet fortified wine from Portugal and a blue cheese from the English Midlands became the classic British Christmas finale. Here is how trade wars, coaching inns and the calendar brought them together.

item.title: Phylloxera: the Tiny Louse That Nearly Killed European Wine
item.description: In the 1860s an American root aphid began killing France's vines; within decades it had wiped out most of Europe's vineyards, and the cure changed how almost every vine is grown.

item.title: Georgia's Qvevri: 8,000 Years of Wine Fermented in Buried Clay
item.description: Long before Bordeaux or Burgundy, farmers in Georgia were making wine in huge clay jars – a tradition that still lives on in the qvevri, buried in the ground.

item.title: Why We 'Drink a Toast': the Bread-in-the-Glass Origin of the Word
item.description: Before it meant raising a glass, a toast was a slice of spiced, browned bread dropped into wine or ale. Here is how a soggy crust became the world's favourite drinking ritual.

item.title: Noble Rot: How Botrytis Cinerea Gave Us Sauternes and Tokaji
item.description: A grey fungus that ruins most fruit can, in the right autumn mists, turn white grapes into the world's greatest sweet wines. Here is how noble rot works.

item.title: Châteauneuf-du-Pape and the 1954 Ban on Flying Saucers
item.description: In 1954 the mayor of Châteauneuf-du-Pape banned flying saucers from landing among his vines – a tongue-in-cheek decree that is still on the books and even inspired a famous Californian wine.

item.title: Veuve Clicquot: the Widow Who Made Champagne Crystal Clear
item.description: Widowed at 27, Barbe-Nicole Clicquot Ponsardin built a Champagne empire, traded through Napoleon's wars and helped invent the riddling rack that made the wine crystal clear.

item.title: The Speyer Wine Bottle: The Roman Wine Nobody Dares to Open
item.description: Sealed around AD 325 and buried with a Roman couple, the Speyer bottle still holds liquid after some 1,700 years, and its museum has never dared to pull the cork.

item.title: Cabernet Sauvignon's Parents: How DNA Solved a Wine Mystery
item.description: For centuries nobody knew where the world's most famous red grape came from. In 1996 two UC Davis scientists ran a DNA test and found a surprising pair of parents.

item.title: The Judgment of Paris: the day California beat France
item.description: In 1976 a blind tasting in a Paris hotel put two little-known Napa Valley wines above the best of Bordeaux and Burgundy, and changed how the world thinks about wine.
